en.title: Tirabhukti and the early-medieval regional order
en.summary: Tīrabhukti, later Tirhut, became a durable administrative and regional name for north Bihar, but it should not be treated as a timeless replacement for Videha or Mithila. The terms belong to different archives and scales. Videha is prominent in Vedic, Upanishadic, Buddhist, Jain, and epic traditions; Tīrabhukti becomes especially visible in Gupta and early-medieval administrative records; Mithila grows in importance as a literary, scholastic, and regional name whose later reach cannot simply be projected backward.

mai.title: तिरभुक्ति आ आरम्भिक मध्यकालीन क्षेत्रीय व्यवस्था

The Basarh seals and the first firm administrative archive

en.title: The Karnatas and Simraongarh
en.summary: The Karnata polity is best understood as a kingdom whose political geography crossed the modern India–Nepal boundary rather than as a dynasty confined to one present-day national space. Its best-known capital, Simraongarh (Simraungadh), lies in the Nepal Tarai, while its agrarian, religious, intellectual and military field extended southward into the plains of Tirabhukti or Tirhut.

en.title: Oiniwar rule, Sultanate power, and political transition
en.summary: The Oiniwar period should not be introduced as the automatic restoration of a sovereign Mithila kingdom immediately after the fall of the Karnatas. The Tughluq conquest horizon around 1324–25 changed the political scale on which regional authority operated. Local chiefs, learned families, landed intermediaries and religious institutions remained, but they now negotiated in a field that could include Delhi, provincial governors, Jaunpur, Bengal and neighbouring Nepal. The Oiniwar rulers emerged from this field.

en.title: Two Vidyāpatis: Maithili, Sanskrit learning, and law
en.summary: This history adopts a two-Vidyāpati reconstruction as a governing rule of attribution. Mahākavi Vidyāpati is treated as the earlier, pre-Jyotirīśvara poet of the Maithili Padāvalī tradition. Vidyāpati Ṭhakkura is treated as the later Oiniwar-period intellectual associated with Sanskrit and Avahaṭṭa works, including Kīrtilatā, Kīrtipatākā, Puruṣaparīkṣā and Likhanāvalī. The distinction is applied throughout the book to chronology, language, patronage, caste claims, legends, bibliography, glossary and index.

en.title: Mughal-era Tirhut, Anga, and early-modern institutions
en.summary: The sixteenth century did not replace a bounded medieval kingdom with a uniformly administered Mughal province in a single act. North Bihar, the Ganga corridor, the Munger-Bhagalpur zone, Purnea, and the Himalayan-facing frontier entered Mughal political structures through conquest, appointments, fiscal assessment, military service, and accommodation with entrenched local power-holders.
